for peptides presented by class I MHC proteins could be improved by considering features encoded by the structure of the peptide/MHC complex, rather than by features of the peptide amino acid sequence alone. Our hypothesis was predicated on the notion that immunogenicity is inﬂuenced by both peptide binding to the MHC protein as well as TCR binding to the peptide/MHC complex. Prediction methods for the former are well-developed, whereas prediction methods for the latter are in their infancy. Some peptide features that possibly promote TCR binding have been identiﬁed (13–17), but we suggest these and other important features are best interpreted, and ultimately predicted, by examining structures and their physicochemical properties and energies. Identifying these features and the magnitudes required are particularly important for tumor neoantigens, as the bar for establishing “diﬀerence from self” for neoantigens is higher than for antigens from viruses or other pathogens due to the various tolerance mechanisms that limit self-reactivity. To explore our hypothesis, we developed a rapid and accurate procedure for modeling the structures of nonamers bound to the class I MHC protein HLA-A2. Our procedure performed well-compared to previously published methods and was suitably rapid for use with large peptide databases. Following this, we assembled a database of immunogenic and

non-immunogenic peptides, including in the latter HLA-A2- incompatible peptides predicted to be very weak binders. We used the structural modeling procedure to model the nearly 4,000 peptide/HLA-A2 complexes in this database. We then trained an artiﬁcial neural network for predicting immunogenicity that relied on energetic features determined by the structures. As potential terms to be incorporated, we included features such as van der Waals interactions, hydrophobic solvation, Coulombic potentials, hydrogen bond energies, side chain rotamer energies, as well as solvent accessible surface areas. We designed our approach to capture both peptide binding to the MHC protein as well as TCR binding to the peptide/MHC, as both are determined by structural and physicochemical features, and in determining immunogenicity, strong TCR binding can compensate for weak peptide-MHC binding and vice versa (11, 12, 36). Our structural approach outperformed other prediction tools, including comparisons with sequence-based neural networks trained on the same peptide datasets. Our model also outperformed publicly available immunogenicity prediction tools, as well as predictions based on peptide-MHC binding aﬃnity. Beyond immunogenicity prediction, an important added beneﬁt of our approach is the availability of structural models to aid in interpreting results. The utility of these models is found when comparing results for mutant peptides and their wild-type

counterparts, as the models can indicate the types of structural alterations that impact TCR recognition of a mutated vs. wildtype peptide/MHC complex. In cases in which the mutation improves immunogenicity by enhancing peptide binding to the MHC protein, the models still provide indications about which peptide features may be important for TCR recognition. A key observation that emerged from our analysis is that, excluding non-HLA-A2 binders, immunogenic peptides possessed higher total energies than non-immunogenic complexes. We believe this result is an important indicator of how structure and energy can inﬂuence immunogenicity beyond simply enhancing peptide aﬃnity for the MHC protein: amino acid substitutions that impart a higher energy onto a peptide/MHC complex yield ligands that have more energy to release upon TCR binding, thus translating into stronger TCR binding aﬃnities. Higher energy would, for example, be imparted by removing exposed charges or increasing exposed hydrophobic surface area. Given a compatible TCR, this high energy would be released upon binding, contributing to a favorable TCR-peptide/MHC binding free energy, i.e., better TCR binding aﬃnity. From this interpretation, neoantigens have a greater likelihood of being immunogenic not simply when they are chemically or structurally “diﬀerent” from a corresponding wild-type peptide, but diﬀerent in ways that promote strong TCR binding. In addition to helping explain immunogenicity, this interpretation connects immunogenicity to well-understood physical attributes of biomolecular recognition, and is consistent with studies on the composition and structural properties of protein-protein interfaces and how they diﬀer from other protein surfaces, as well as the properties of “hot spots” in protein-protein interfaces (63, 64). Although we consider our results promising, improvements are necessary before a structural modeling/energetic scoring methodology can be widely deployed. Our rapid modeling procedure, while matching or even exceeding the performance of previous approaches, did not capture all the observed structural changes that occur in response to peptide modiﬁcation. We expect that incorporating more exhaustive conformational sampling will yield superior models. Although this will increase computational time, this impact will be oﬀset by ongoing improvements in computing hardware and sampling methods. Growth in the number of crystallographic structures of peptides bound to class I MHC proteins, particularly structures of closely related peptide pairs, will help benchmark the accuracy of structural modeling. Our study was limited to nonamers and HLA-A2, primarily because of the large amount of structural and immunological data available for nonamer/HLA-A2 complexes. In the absence of more structural data, extension to peptides of other lengths and other HLA haplotypes will call for even more sophisticated modeling. Another area for methodological improvements is in the energy functions and other terms used to evaluate peptide/MHC models. We relied upon an energy function and set of terms frequently used in the analysis and design of protein structures. As with modeling procedures, more

complex means to assess protein structures and energies are available, and these undergo regular reﬁnements. Incorporation of additional or more sophisticated energetic terms (e.g., electrostatic surface potentials, more accurate approaches to computing solvation energies, and consideration of changes in peptide ﬂexibility that occur upon mutation) could thus also be explored. Attention should also be focused toward generating datasets that can be used to train models aiming to predict peptide immunogenicity (65). Epitopes with veriﬁed, strong immune responses can be found in the IEDB as we relied upon here, and eﬀorts such as the Cancer Antigenic Peptide Database aim to tabulate immunogenic neoantigens (66). However, experimentally validated immunogenic neoantigens remain rare, and some eﬀorts aimed at building CTL epitope databases prioritize peptide processing and MHC presentation over T cell recognition (67). Additionally, prediction tools also require knowledge of non-immunogenic epitopes, particularly those that bind well to MHC proteins yet do not favor TCR binding. We relied on a list of self-peptides which we hypothesized would be dominated by such epitopes, but to some extent would also include ones that are well-recognized by TCRs. This would include not only self-peptides that would drive negative selection, but as our peptide list was derived from immortalized HeLa cells (52, 53), it also likely includes various HPV epitopes and associated neoantigens. The fact that we recovered previously identiﬁed positional diﬀerences in hydrophobicity between immunogenic and nonimmunogenic peptides suggests that the inﬂuence of such peptides in our self-dataset is small. However, a better accounting of peptides (ideally derived from healthy tissues) which bind well to class I MHC proteins yet do not promote strong immunogenicity when tested across multiple T cell populations is needed. Lastly, our prediction eﬀorts were centered on the ability to elicit strong CD8+ T cell responses. Eliciting CD8+ T cell responses remains a goal of peptide-based vaccine eﬀorts for both pathogens and cancer (68), and CD8+

T cell activity is associated with antitumor immunity (69). However, additional factors will inﬂuence successful peptide-based vaccines. A deeper understanding of the strengths and types of responses associated with successful antitumor immunity will further allow prediction eﬀorts to improve. In conclusion, we have explored the potential for largescale structure-based modeling and energetic scoring for predicting peptide immunogenicity, with an emphasis on cancer neoantigens. Our approach outperformed other approaches and although it is a proof-of-concept, the avenues for improvement are clear and actionable. The structural modeling allows for insights into immunogenicity lacking from other approaches. Furthermore, because it is fully atomistic, the approach can grow to incorporate complexities not addressable via sequence considerations alone, such as those arising from peptides incorporating post translational modiﬁcations or non-standard amino acids.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

Structural Modeling of HLA-A2 Presented Peptides Structural modeling of peptide/HLA-A2 complexes was performed with PyRosetta using the Talaris2014 energy function (38, 39). The desired peptide sequence was computationally introduced into HLA-A2, using PDB IDs 1DUZ, 3QFD, and 5FA3 as templates (40–42). This was followed by 50 Monte Carlo-based simulated annealing sidechain and peptide backbone minimization steps using the LoopMover_Reﬁne_CCD protocol, generating 10 independent decoys per peptide from each starting template. The large number of resulting packing operations introduced some minor variability when scoring the models. Therefore, the unweighted score terms for the three lowest scoring trajectories were averaged and used for neural network inputs. Solvent accessible surface area calculations were performed with PyRosetta and Discovery Studio using a 1.4 Å radius probe. The modeling procedure is available as Supplementary File 1.

Dataset Collection Our structural database for evaluating modeling strategies consisted of high resolution (<3.0 Å) nonameric peptide/HLA- A2 structures within the PDB. Structures in this dataset were selected for strong electron density as determined by visual inspection using Coot for calculating 2Fo-Fc density maps (70). Our ﬁnal database contained 53 structures presenting diﬀerent peptide epitopes. The neural network training set contained 3,955 nonameric peptides collected from published sources. For self-peptides categorized as non-immunogenic we used lists of peptides identiﬁed via mass spectrometry analysis of human HeLa cells transfected with soluble HLA-A2 (52, 53). HLA-A2 incompatible nonamers were obtained from IEDB training sets (24). Immunogenic peptides were selected from IEDB to ensure quality of data and minimize false positives by selecting only HLA-A2-restricted nonamers with a positive IFNγ ELISpot with a response frequency starting at 50. The test dataset was derived from a recent review of neoantigens (60), again selecting only nonamers presented by HLA- A2 for evaluation, resulting in a dataset consisting of 291 candidate neoantigens.

## ARTIFICIAL NEURAL NETWORK TRAINING

Two-layer feed-forward networks were trained with the scaled conjugate gradient back-propagation trainscg tool in MATLAB 2017b. Training and evaluation of neural network architectures was performed using a nested 5- fold cross-validation procedure (23). The peptides in the training dataset were randomly split into ﬁve sets of training, validation, and test data. The splitting was performed such that all sets had approximately the same distribution of non-binding, self, and immunogenic peptides. With the binary classiﬁcation of immunogenic or non-immunogenic

(with non-immunogenic incorporating self and non-binding peptides), the training data were used to perform feedforward and back propagation. The validation set deﬁned the stopping criteria for the network training, and the test set evaluated performance via AUC. Sets were rotated to ensure each was used in training, validation, and testing. To maintain an equal distribution of classiﬁers and eliminate bias for non-immunogenic peptides, immunogenic peptides in the training sets, but not testing or validation sets, were randomly oversampled. The structure-based neural network architecture used was a conventional feed-forward network with an input layer containing 80–117 neurons, one hidden layer with 1–10 neurons, and a single neuron output layer. The neurons in the input layer describe structural and structure-derived energetic features of the nine amino acids in the peptide sequence, with each amino acid represented by up to 11 neurons. The remaining 18 neurons describe global structural and structure-derived energetic features of the entire peptide/HLA-A2 complex. The structural and energetic features were those that comprise the Talaris2014 energy function (39) or derived from the structure as listed in Table S3 [described in (56)]. For each of the ﬁve training and test sets, a series of network trainings were performed each with a diﬀerent number of hidden neurons (2, 3, 4, 6, 8, and 10) and a diﬀerent number of input neurons. Finally, a single network with the highest test performance was selected. For control networks that considered peptide sequence or amino acid hydropathy values, we encoded peptide sequences in 20 × 9 sparse matrices encoding peptide sequence or 1 × 9 matrices containing Wimley-White hydropathy values (55) corresponding to the amino acid at each position. These matrices were used to train networks of the same architecture (except they relied on 180 or 9 input nodes) subject to the same cross validation procedure.

Protein Crystallization and Structure Determination Puriﬁed complexes of ILNAMIVKI, ILNAMIAKI, and ILNAMITKI with HLA-A2 were generated by refolding recombinant heavy chain and β2-microglobulin from bacteriallyproduced inclusion bodies according to standard procedures (71), followed by puriﬁcation using anion exchange and size-exclusion chromatography. Peptides were synthesized commercially by AAPTEC at >90% purity. Crystals of the ILNAMIVKI complex were grown by hanging-drop vapor diﬀusion at 23◦C in 20% PEG 8000, 100 mM MES pH 6.5, 200 mM magnesium acetate. # Accurate and well-powered case–control analysis of spatial molecular data

Yakir A. Reshef 1,2,3,4 , Lakshay Sood1,2,3,4, Michelle Curtis 1,2,3,4, Laurie Rumker1,2,3,4,5, Daniel J. Stein 1,2,3,4,5, Mukta G. Palshikar1,2,3,4, Saba Nayar6,7, Andrew Filer6, Anna Helena Jonsson8, Ilya Korsunsky 1,2,3,4 & Soumya Raychaudhuri 1,2,3,4,5

As spatial molecular data grow in scope, there is a pressing need to identify disease-associated spatial structures. Current approaches typically make restrictive assumptions such as representing tissue regions by abundances of discrete cell types and samples by abundances of discrete niches; this risks overlooking important signals. Here we introduce variational inference-based microniche analysis (VIMA), a method combining deep learning with principled statistics to discover disease-associated spatial features with greater flexibility and precision. VIMA trains an ensemble of variational autoencoders to summarize the contents of every small tissue patch in a dataset via numeric ‘fingerprints’. It uses these to define many data-dependent, overlapping ‘microniches’ and meta-analyzes them to identify microniches whose abundance correlates significantly with case− control status. We confirm VIMA’s calibration, power and spatial accuracy in simulations. We then apply VIMA to spatial datasets spanning three diseases and spatial modalities, recapitulating known biology and identifying new spatial features of disease.

Spatial profiling of tissue samples has long been a foundational tool in biology1,2 and is now a pillar of biomedical research3–6. In recent years, the scale and richness of spatial molecular modalities have dramatically increased, and modern modalities now profile scores of proteins and thousands of genes at high spatial resolution7–14; however, this richness complicates systematic analysis, and traditional approaches in cancer15,16 and elsewhere17 have relied on manually constructed scoring systems. This limits discoveries to those that fit existing paradigms and scales poorly as more genes and proteins are assayed. Thus, the development of new computational methods for high-resolution annotation of tissue structures in spatial molecular

data has become an active area of research. Modern methods based on local abundances of different cell types16,18,19, spatially constrained clustering20 and aggregation21,22, spatial factorization23,24, graph neural networks25–27 and others28–30 have enabled identification of granular tissue structures. More recent work has begun to explore the intuition that neural network architectures from image analysis can be built upon to provide powerful and flexible tissue representations31–33. Here, we focus specifically on the question of statistical case− control analysis in spatial data: given a spatial dataset with multiple case and control samples, are there patterns that are statistically significantly different between cases and controls, after multiple-testing

VIMA takes as input a multi-sample spatial molecular dataset of any kind as well as sample-level case−control status and covariates such as patient age or sex. VIMA outputs (1) a tensor of samples by microniches by autoencoders called the microniche abundance tensor (MAT) that summarizes the abundance patterns of different microniches across the samples; (2) a global P value indicating the statistical significance of the aggregate spatial differences between case samples and control samples; and (3) a subset of tissue patches whose microniches drive this association at a specified FDR threshold, with a directional effect size for each patch. VIMA’s results can be represented on a consensus nearest-neighbor graph of tissue patches that can be visualized with Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP). To create the patch fingerprints, VIMA rasterizes each sample, performs dimensionality reduction to convert the spatial markers into a smaller set of ‘meta-markers’ (Methods), and uses a sliding window to convert samples into sets of overlapping, square tissue patches (Fig. 1a). It then uses the patches to train an ensemble of ten conditional variational autoencoders34 (cVAEs) with identical ResNet18-style architectures35 but different initial weights; each cVAE learns one numerical latent representation (the ‘fingerprint’; Fig. 1b) per patch while being incentivized to remove sample-specific effects (Methods). We use multiple cVAEs because independent training runs yield non-negligible variability in latent representations (Supplementary Fig. 1), and combining them improves power and reproducibility (Supplementary Fig. 2). To define microniches, VIMA builds on our previous work in single-cell analysis36. For each cVAE, it constructs a nearest-neighbor graph of the patch fingerprints (Fig. 1c). For each patch p and each cVAE E, VIMA then defines a microniche anchored at p as follows: each patch p’ belongs to the microniche in proportion to the probability that a random walk in E’s nearest-neighbor graph from p’ reaches p (Methods and Fig. 1c). The goal is for patches more similar to p to have higher membership. VIMA uses microniches to compute a MAT whose n,p,k-th entry is the fraction of patches from sample n in the microniche anchored at patch p defined by the k-th cVAE (Fig. 1d). This is analogous to computing cluster abundances, but with many overlapping microniches and with a different set of microniches for each cVAE. VIMA meta-analyzes the MAT across the cVAEs (Fig. 1e) to perform both a ‘global’ and a ‘local’ association test. The global test tests overall association with case−control status, while the local test identifies patches whose microniches drive the association (Fig. 1f). For the local test, VIMA computes the correlation between microniche abundance and case−control status, then uses adaptive weighted averaging to meta-analyze the ten correlations for each patch into a single ‘microniche coefficient’ in units of correlation (Fig. 1e). It estimates empirical FDRs by computing null distributions with permuted sample labels (Fig. 1f). For the global test, the per-microniche correlations are combined into a single aggregate statistic across the entire MAT, with significance again assessed by permutation (Fig. 1f). Both tests can control for sample-level confounders such as demographic and technical variables (Methods). We confirmed type I error control in simulations (Supplementary Fig. 3) and quantified power and spatial accuracy in detecting spiked-in case−control signals in real data (Supplementary Fig. 4 and Methods). VIMA requires no pretraining so can be used out-of-the-box on new datasets and technologies. It requires minimal parameter tuning and has favorable runtime: for the three datasets analyzed in this paper, which contain S = 27, S = 42 and S = 75 samples, respectively, total runtime including preprocessing was ~2 h, ~2 h and ~8 h, respectively, on a single GPU. We have released open-source software implementing the method.

Identifying spatial features of rheumatoid arthritis subtypes using immunofluorescence microscopy data RA is an inflammatory disease affecting up to 1% of the population in which immune infiltration alters the synovium, leading to tissue

correction? One simple strategy is to annotate the samples in such a dataset with a modern tissue-annotation method, use the annotations to cluster regions of tissue into ‘niches’ with similar biology, and then to test for differential abundance of the niches in cases versus controls; however, while this approach has been used successfully to find case− control associations16,19,21,22,32, it may be under-powered if the tissue annotation is not sufficiently expressive, if the case−control differences are obfuscated by the hard clustering step, or if the tissue annotation is too sensitive to sample-specific idiosyncrasies. To address this challenge, we introduce variational inference-based microniche analysis (VIMA), a method for statistical case−control analysis of spatial molecular data. VIMA uses neural network-based techniques from image processing to learn compact, informative ‘fingerprints’ for each of many small tissue patches in a spatial dataset, similarly to some recent methods32,33; however, VIMA introduces three innovations. First, it uses a conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) architecture designed to learn fingerprints that are minimally influenced by sample- or batch-specific effects, thereby enhancing sensitivity to true case−control signals. Second, VIMA leverages the stochasticity of neural network optimization by training an ensemble of cVAEs rather than just one, resulting in multiple representations that can capture complementary aspects of the same dataset while also increasing replicability. Third, rather than using the fingerprints to cluster the tissue patches into discrete groups, VIMA instead defines many small, potentially overlapping groups of highly similar tissue patches, which we term microniches, and quantifies the abundance of each microniche in each sample. VIMA then performs statistical tests to identify nontrivial correlations between the abundances of the microniches and case−control status, meta-analyzing across the ensemble of cVAEs. VIMA produces both a global statistical test for the presence of any case−control difference in the spatial data as well as a local statistical test identifying the set of specific patches explaining that difference at a given false discovery rate (FDR) threshold. VIMA can be applied to any spatially resolved molecular technology, is well powered even at the modest sample sizes typical of research cohorts, and avoids traditional, parameter-intensive preprocessing steps such as cell segmentation, clustering of cells into discrete cell types, or clustering of tissue regions into discrete niches. VIMA produces properly calibrated P values and so can be used for statistical hypothesis testing, a fact that we confirm in simulations. We apply VIMA to three spatial molecular case−control datasets containing four case−control signals and generated with three different technologies in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) (seven-marker immunofluorescence microscopy), ulcerative colitis (UC) (52-marker CODEX) and dementia (140-gene MERFISH). In each case, VIMA identifies spatial features that differ significantly between cases and controls and that both recapitulate known biology and provide new insights. We also benchmark VIMA against seven state-of-the-art methods and find that most of VIMA’s signals are not detectable with these methods. Finally, we show, using an ablation study, that each new component of VIMA is necessary for its performance.

Results Overview of methods VIMA is based on three central concepts. First, we use a deep-learning architecture common in image analysis (augmented to account for sample-specific spatial artifacts) to represent each tissue patch in a dataset with a numerical ‘fingerprint’ summarizing its essential biology. Second, we take advantage of the stochasticity of neural network training to generate ten sets of these fingerprints, increasing our sensitivity to underlying biology, while simultaneously improving replicability. Third, rather than using the fingerprints to cluster tissue patches into discrete, nonoverlapping groups, we instead define many small, overlapping groups of highly similar tissue patches called ‘microniches’ that form the basic unit of association testing.

We applied VIMA to a seven-marker immunofluorescence (IF) microscopy dataset of S = 27 synovial biopsies from N = 22 patients with RA collected by the Accelerating Medicines Partnership Rheumatoid Arthritis and Systemic Lupus Erythematosus consortium38 (Supplementary Table 1 shows the list of markers profiled). The original publication used a larger cohort (N = 70) with ~20,000 genes profiled by single-cell RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) to group the samples into six ‘cell-type abundance phenotypes’ (CTAPs). Given the limited size of the smaller IF cohort, we grouped CTAPs into three fibroblast-rich ‘stromal’ types and three T/B/myeloid-rich ‘immune’ types. This grouping was motivated by the emerging role of fibroblasts in RA39,40 and their association with poor treatment response38. Before using VIMA to test for association to stromal versus immune status, we first evaluated its patch fingerprints and microniches. The autoencoders reconstructed tissue patches with an average mean-squared error of 0.57, improving over baselines of 1.00 (guessing dataset-wide average for all pixels) and 0.75 (guessing patch-average expression). Figure 2a shows an example reconstruction from a single cVAE. The fingerprints also effectively accounted for sample-specific

idiosyncrasies: we quantified local sample mixing using perplexity across samples of each patch’s fingerprint-based nearest neighbors. VIMA produced substantially higher perplexities than other methods, including neural network-based methods (Fig. 2b and Methods). Because this dataset lacks cell segmentation, we benchmarked only three of seven methods; the others require segmented cells and are evaluated in subsequent datasets. On visual inspection, microniches generated by VIMA’s autoencoders exhibit consistent biological features (Fig. 2c). In one arbitrarily selected autoencoder, we observed microniches containing: broad CD34-high staining with interspersed CLIC5-high areas, likely representing CD34+/CD90− sublining fibroblasts near lining fibroblasts; large CLIC5-high, CD34-low regions indicative of lining fibroblasts; CLIC5-high areas with blurred texture and interspersed 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI); boundaries between CLIC5-high and CLIC5-low/DAPI-high regions; DAPI saturation likely reflecting artifact; DAPI-high infiltrates surrounding CD34-high regions that are likely blood vessels; and perivascular CD90-high staining representing pericytes or CD90+ fibroblasts. We next asked whether VIMA could ‘rediscover’ the stromal versus immune distinction found in the larger single-cell cohort, without previous labels. We applied principal-component analysis (PCA) to the MAT and found that sample loadings along the first two principal components (PCs) nearly perfectly separate stromal samples from immune samples (Fig. 3a). Thus, despite using only seven markers from 22 donors (rather than ~20,000 genes from 70 donors in the original analysis), VIMA leverages spatial information to reveal this important source of biological variation. We then applied VIMA’s local and global tests to compare stromal and immune samples. VIMA identified a strong case−control difference (P = 2.0 × 10−4) with 5,222 of 10,345 patches significant at FDR 10% (Fig. 3b). Reassuringly, stromal-associated patches were higher in CLIC5 (a marker of lining fibroblasts) and the immune-associated patches were higher in CD3 (T cells), CD68 (macrophages) and DAPI (nucleated cells; Supplementary Fig. 5), recapitulating expected biology. In contrast, we did not detect this immune-versus-stromal difference using discrete tissue annotations from other benchmarked methods (Fig. 3c and Methods). We next examined the spatial distribution of the VIMA-annotated stromal and immune patches within each sample. Although each sample received a single overall label from the nonspatial single-cell data, immune-labeled samples often contained both stromal- and immune-like regions that were spatially segregated (Fig. 3d). Thus, synovial cells form spatially organized communities with distinct biology not captured by sample-wide cell-type abundances. This spatial characterization advances our understanding of how spatial interactions

among cell types contribute to this disease and challenges the notion of a single disease subtype per patient, with possible implications for precision medicine in RA. We also found biological heterogeneity among stromal- and immune-associated patches. Using Leiden clustering41 on patch fingerprints, we grouped immune-associated patches into two subtypes (Fig. 3e and Methods): one highly cellular, with strong DAPI staining and a T cell infiltrate (Fig. 3e (cluster 1) and Supplementary Fig. 6), and another with spatially proximal CD68-high (macrophage) and CD90-high (sublining fibroblast) regions with T cell aggregates (Fig. 3e (cluster 2) and Supplementary Fig. 6). Similarly, stromal-associated patches formed two subtypes (Fig. 3f): one with strong CD34 staining (sublining fibroblasts and/or endothelial cells; Fig. 3f (cluster 3) and Supplementary Fig. 7) and another with strong CLIC5 staining (lining fibroblasts; Fig. 3f (cluster 4) and Supplementary Fig. 7). We found strong associations between these clusters and two of the six original disease subtypes (the CTAPs). Among immune-associated clusters, cluster 1 was more prevalent than cluster 2 in the ‘myeloid’ (M) CTAP (log odds ratio (OR) 0.73, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.95) and less prevalent in the ‘T cell/myeloid’ (TM) CTAP (log OR −0.91, 95% CI −1.18 to −0.65; Fig. 3g). Among stromal-associated clusters, cluster 3 was more prevalent than cluster 4 in the M CTAP (log OR 1.16, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.65) and less prevalent in the TM CTAP (log OR −2.07, 95% CI −3.01 to −1.13; Fig. 3h). Identifying effects of TNF inhibition on lymphoid aggregates in ulcerative colitis using CODEX data UC is a chronic inflammatory disease of the colonic mucosa causing diarrhea, abdominal pain and rectal bleeding42. Inhibition of tumor necrosis factor (TNF) has become a cornerstone of treatment42, but response varies and its molecular determinants remain unclear43. To identify the spatial consequences of TNF inhibition, we applied VIMA to a 52-marker CODEX8 dataset of S = 42 colonic biopsies from N = 34 patients (29 with UC and 5 healthy)19 (Supplementary Table 2 shows a list of profiled markers). We first used VIMA to distinguish UC from healthy samples and found a strong association (global P = 1.7 × 10−3) with 11,839 of 21,359 patches significant at FDR 10% (4,146 UC-associated, 7,693 healthy-associated; Fig. 4a). UC-associated patches localized deep to epithelial layers, consistent with known disease biology44,45 (Fig. 4b), and showed higher levels of immune markers including CD3 (T cells), CD19 (B cells) and CD45 (immune cells; Fig. 4c). Unlike with the RA case−control analysis, the UC-versus-healthy signal was also detectable using tissue annotations generated using UTAG21 and post-Harmony46 patchwide average expression profile (Fig. 4d), though VIMA achieved substantially higher statistical significance. In addition, VIMA was the only method that detected UC-associated patches and not just healthy-associated patches, enabling analysis of TNF inhibition effects in diseased tissue (Fig. 4e). We focused subsequent analyses on these 4,146 UC-associated patches detected by VIMA. To study TNF inhibition effects, we used VIMA to conduct case− control analysis within UC-associated patches, comparing patients treated with TNF inhibition in the past (‘prior/chronicTNFi’) to patients with either no TNF inhibition at all or recent TNF inhibition only (‘never/newTNFi’; Methods). We found a strong association (global P = 1.5 × 10−3) with 2,307 of the 4,146 patches significant at FDR 10% (Fig. 4f). Subclustering the UC-associated patches into two clusters (Methods) and comparing abundances yielded similar results (P = 5.6 × 10−3 by t-test; Supplementary Fig. 9), with one cluster strongly enriched for positively associated patches and the other for negatively associated patches (Supplementary Fig. 10). The fraction of associated patches per sample further stratified patients by TNF exposure in a dose-response-like gradient, ranging from longstanding TNF inhibition to previous (but not current) TNF inhibition, recent initiation of TNF inhibition and finally no TNF inhibition (Fig. 4g). Prior/chronicTNFi-associated patches shared features with both healthy and UC tissue: they showed lower levels of B and T cell markers, similar to healthy-associated patches, but higher fibroblast, macrophage and mesenchymal markers (CD54, CD90, CD34 and MMP12; Fig. 4h), similar to UC-associated patches (Fig. 4c). Comparing microniche coefficients confirmed this signal (Supplementary Fig. 11). Spatially, never/newTNFi-associated patches exhibited B cell aggregates with surrounding T cells, consistent with lymphoid aggregates, whereas chronic/priorTNFi-associated patches showed a spatially disorganized pattern of mesenchymal markers intermixed with scant lymphocytes (Fig. 4i). These findings suggest TNF inhibition remodels colonic architecture (potentially in a long-lasting way) by reducing lymphoid aggregates and increasing mesenchymal and fibroblast activity. Our results extend previous analysis of this dataset19, which used a cell-type-based workflow requiring segmentation, cell-type annotation and clustering of spatial regions into ‘cellular neighborhoods’. In a subgroup of UC with intermediate-grade colonic inflammation, this strategy identified a modest negative association (P < 0.01) between TNF inhibition and a lymphoid aggregate-associated neighborhood, but this was limited to one patient subset and was not corrected for multiple testing across patient subsets and cellular neighborhoods. In contrast, VIMA identifies a robust reduction in lymphoid structures in

TNF-treated patients without segmentation, cell-type annotation, or patient subset selection, providing stronger evidence that TNF inhibition disrupts lymphoid aggregation in colonic tissue.

Identifying dementia-associated tissue structures using spatial transcriptomics data Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia in older patients47. Single-cell RNA-seq has identified cell populations with altered abundance in patients with Alzheimer’s disease48, but the spatial structures underlying dementia remain difficult to study. We applied VIMA to a 140-gene MERFISH dataset of S = 75 postmortem medial temporal gyrus samples from N = 27 patients48 (15 with Alzheimer’s disease or Alzheimer’s disease-related dementia) containing 516 million transcripts (Supplementary Table 3 contains a list of profiled genes). VIMA detected a significant association to dementia status (global P = 5.4 × 10−3), with 27,072 out of 70,898 patches significant at FDR 5% (Fig. 5a), despite modest sample size compared to the analogous single-cell dataset. The signal was strong: the fraction of dementia-versus-control-associated patches in each sample nearly separates dementia from control samples (Fig. 5b). In contrast, we did not detect this association using annotations generated by other spatial methods (Fig. 5c). A nonspatial analysis using sample-wide cell-type proportions was also null, indicating that spatial information reduces the sample size needed to detect this association (Supplementary Fig. 12). The associated patches map to cortical architecture and reveal both known and new biology. Control-associated patches colocalize very well with cortical layers 2 and 3 (Fig. 5d), suggesting thinning of these layers in dementia and consistent with previous histology49, omics48,50 and neuroimaging51 studies as well as with a nonspatial single-cell analysis of a much larger (N = 84) superset of this cohort48. We additionally confirmed this by annotating patches with abundant layer 2/3 neurons (Methods), observing depletion in dementia (P = 5.7 × 10−4 by a one-sided Kolmogorov–Smirnov test; Fig. 5e), validating recovery of known biology. Clustering dementia-associated patches revealed two clusters localizing to different subregions of layer 6 (superficial layer 6 and the layer 6-white matter interface; Supplementary Fig. 13) and with different cell-type compositions (Supplementary Figs. 14 and 15) but similar associations to dementia (Supplementary Fig. 16). These subtypes may reflect distinct pathological processes. In contrast, the dementia-associated patches identified by VIMA are new. They localize to the deepest cortical layer (layer 6b) but are not uniformly distributed within that layer (Fig. 5d). Compared to other layer 6b patches, they are enriched for oligodendrocytes (1.33× enrichment, P < 1 × 10−4 by donor-level permutation test) and depleted for L6 IT Car3 neurons (0.40× depletion, P < 1 × 10−4 by donor-level permutation test; Fig. 5f and Supplementary Table 4). These differences are not explained by variation in overall L6b neuron abundance (Fig. 5f and Supplementary Table 4). Manual annotation of patches with high L6b neuron and oligodendrocyte abundance (Methods) reproduced the enrichment (P = 1.7 × 10−3 by one-sided Kolmogorov– Smirnov test; Fig. 5g). These results suggest a previously unrecognized oligodendrocyte-rich niche in layer 6b that is more abundant in dementia. Oligodendrocytes have recently been shown to produce amyloid-β in the cortex52,53 and have been implicated in dementia pathogenesis54, though protective roles have also been reported54. The enrichment of oligodendrocytes in dementia-associated layer 6b patches suggests that their protective versus deleterious effects may depend on spatial context, with amyloidogenic activity potentially localized to layer 6b near white matter. This would be consistent with evidence that myelin dysfunction drives amyloid-β deposition55. Our findings therefore highlight the importance of spatial heterogeneity in oligodendrocyte function and underscore the value of spatially resolved studies of cortical architecture in dementia.

For the coarser RA and UC signals, neural network architecture and microniche-based analysis were most important, whereas for the subtler TNFi and dementia signals, removal of sample-specific bias further improved power, likely via better integration of tissue representations. To assess the roles of patch- and sample-level representations, we performed an additional ablation study using three synthetic phenotypes spiked into a downsampled dementia dataset; the phenotypes are shown graphically in Supplementary Fig. 17. Using a simplified VIMA-like model with a single representation for ease of simulation, we reduced the richness of the patch-level representation in a stepwise way, starting from a VIMA-like autoencoder, then moving to a two-layer convolutional network, to a PCA-based representation and then to patch-average expression. Reduced representation richness led to decreased power in both global and local tests and reduced spatial accuracy (Supplementary Figs. 17 and 18). Replacing microniche-based sample representations with cluster-based ones further decreased power and spatial accuracy (Supplementary Fig. 19). Assessing sample-level integration in simulation is challenging due to difficulty simulating realistic technical artifacts. We therefore evaluated integration across all datasets and benchmarked methods, finding that VIMA’s cVAEs achieved the highest integration on average, followed by CANVAS, CellCharter and TissueMosaic (Fig. 6b). Reducing integration in simulations by weakening the variational penalty decreased power and spatial accuracy (Supplementary Fig. 20). Together, these results indicate that well-powered case−control analysis requires rich patch-level embeddings, strong sample integration and rich sample-level representations beyond discrete clusters.

Discussion Here we introduced VIMA, a method for statistical case−control analysis of spatial molecular data across a range of modalities, from low-content proteomics through spatial transcriptomics. VIMA uses an ensemble of conditional variational autoencoders to extract numerical fingerprints for each patch of tissue in a dataset that summarize the biology of that patch, then defines overlapping groups of similar patches (‘microniches’), and finally tests whether their abundance correlates with case− control status. VIMA outputs (1) a tensor of samples by microniches by autoencoders called the MAT summarizing the abundance patterns of different microniches across the samples; (2) a global P value for association to case−control status; and (3) a subset of associated patches at

a specified FDR, with effect sizes. VIMA accounts for sample-specific artifacts, supports covariates, requires minimal parameter tuning, and runs efficiently even on datasets with hundreds of millions of transcripts. VIMA is different from the deep-learning-based methods popular in digital pathology56,57, which typically are trained on thousands or even millions of patient samples and focus on patient-level prediction of disease status rather than defining disease-associated spatial structures at specified FDRs in small research cohorts. We applied VIMA to three datasets across distinct spatial modalities and identified new biological signals, including detailed characterization of RA disease subtypes and spatial heterogeneity of rheumatoid arthritis synovium, a spatial signature of TNF inhibition in UC, and a new dementia-associated tissue niche in postmortem brain samples. Benchmarking showed these signals are largely undetectable using tissue representations from current state-of-the-art methods. Ablation studies further demonstrated that VIMA’s key ingredients (rich patch representations, avoidance of sample-specific bias and microniche-based sample representations) are all required for its performance. In benchmarking, we used each tissue representation to cluster spatial units into ‘niches’ then tested each niche for association with multiple-testing correction (Supplementary Fig. 21). Variations on this strategy, such as testing the clusters with a global test statistic akin to VIMA’s global test, cross-sample harmonization or using the representations in a VIMA-like microniche framework, yielded only modest improvements, with VIMA retaining superior performance (Supplementary Figs. 22–24). Thus, both the way patch fingerprints are constructed and the way they are used are important for VIMA’s performance. We emphasize, however, that most benchmarked methods were designed for tissue annotation rather than case−control analysis and perform well for that purpose. Our benchmarking does not assess annotation accuracy within samples, but rather the extent to which such representations support inter-sample case−control analysis, focusing on metrics such as perplexity, power to detect case−control differences and number of significant patches identified. VIMA treats spatial data as images without requiring segmentation into cells, cell types and tissue regions. This enables use across spatial modalities, avoids error-prone discretization and reduces user-dependent parameter choices (for example, number of cell types and tolerance of cell segmentation). It also facilitates simple integration of modalities if available by concatenating marker or gene channels. As this approach develops, incorporating pretrained models,

VIMA differs from many deep-learning-based methods for spatial data by using a variational autoencoder rather than contrastive-learning-based or transformer-based architectures. We chose this simpler framework to keep training time low and to allow us to explicitly incentivize removal of sample-specific technical artifacts without explicitly enumerating what those artifacts are as is the case with contrastive-learning frameworks; however, we hope and expect that future work will reveal architectures better suited for case−control analysis than what we have chosen here. While developing VIMA, we observed that cVAEs trained on the same data produce variable representations due to stochastic training, suggesting that each captures a distinct view of the data (Supplementary Fig. 1). Using an ensemble of ten cVAEs leverages these complementary representations to improve detection of true signal while increasing replicability, with diminishing returns beyond ten models (Supplementary Fig. 2). Because data loading dominates runtime, training ten cVAEs in parallel increases runtime by only ~5× rather than 10×, allowing VIMA’s runtime to stay relatively short despite the training of so many models. VIMA has several limitations. First, although VIMA runs quickly, this requires a GPU; CPU-only use can be slow unless multiple cores are available. Second, dramatically different choices of patch size (for example, 40 μm versus 400 μm in length) may emphasize different types of signals. Third, interpreting VIMA’s results requires downstream analysis; we maintain, however, that as with other genomic modalities this process is always necessary, whether before or after the case−control analysis is performed, and that applying this careful thought after the spatial regions of interest are delineated may be advantageous. In practice, interpretation can be performed using tools such as cell-type annotation, clustering and niche calling, differential expression and marker visualization, and may be complemented by methods for fine-grained spatial annotation such as the ones benchmarked in this study, which could provide biological context for the microniches that VIMA prioritizes. Finally, while VIMA’s flexibility enables detection of diverse signals, targeted methods may outperform it when their assumptions closely match the underlying biology. Despite these limitations, VIMA is a sensitive and accurate way to identify disease-relevant spatial features across a range of spatial modalities by combining deep learning with a rigorous and flexible statistical framework. As spatial datasets grow in size and dimensionality, methods that capture sample-level variation will be increasingly important for translating these data into advances in our understanding of disease.

Methods Variational inference-based microniche analysis Intuition. VIMA is built on two technical concepts: (1) the patch fingerprint, which is a numerical representation of a tissue patch learned by a variational autoencoder that can be used to quantitatively assess the similarity of pairs of patches; and (2) the microniche, which is a small set of tissue patches from multiple samples that are biologically very similar to each other. Broadly, our method proceeds by using the patch fingerprints to construct the microniches and then finding case−control differences by searching for microniches whose abundance correlates with case status in a statistical hypothesis testing framework. In this section, we first establish notation, then describe preprocessing (including pixel-level batch correction), patch fingerprint extraction via conditional variational autoencoders, microniche construction for each autoencoder and statistical association testing with meta-analysis across autoencoders.

Notation and assumptions. Let {S1, ⋯, SN} be a set of N spatial molecular samples with M different markers or genes measured for each sample. We assume that each sample has been rasterized into pixels of size r x r, and we represent each sample SN as a tensor of shape (Xn, Yn, M) whose (x, y, m)-th entry is either the intensity of marker m in the x,y-th pixel (for nontranscript-based modalities) or the total count of gene m in the x,y-th pixel (for transcript-based modalities). For ease of exposition, we occasionally refer below to this number as intensity even for transcript-based modalities. In all analyses in this paper, we set r to be 10 μm; however, smaller values are in principle possible and could reveal aspects of tissue architecture that occur on smaller length scales.

Preprocessing and pixel-level batch correction. VIMA pre-processes data to (1) separate tissue from background; (2) reduce a potentially large number of markers into a more manageable set of ‘meta-markers;’ and (3) remove sample- or batch-specific artifacts. To accomplish (1), we summarize the total amount of signal in each pixel in a modality-dependent way, for example, using the total number of transcripts in that pixel (for transcript-based modalities) or the sum of all marker intensities divided by the sum of the intensities of all negative control stains (for nontranscript-based modalities). VIMA then uses this number to segment each slide into foreground (tissue) and background. For transcript-based modalities, VIMA simply applies a threshold of ten transcripts per pixel. For nontranscript-based modalities, in which nonspecific background staining is a prominent feature, VIMA instead uses Otsu thresholding58. Once the foreground is defined, all background pixel intensities are set to 0 for all markers. To accomplish (2), VIMA log-normalizes non-empty pixels using the dataset-wide median total intensity, then averages values within a 5 × 5 neighborhood to form ‘meta-pixels.’ PCA is performed on these to obtain loadings across markers. These loadings are then applied to the original (unsmoothed) pixels to generate K-dimensional meta-marker representations (default K = 10, or K = 5 when fewer markers are available). To accomplish (3), VIMA removes sample-specific and batchspecific artifacts by applying the Harmony algorithm46 with default parameters to the meta-marker representation of all the non-empty pixels in the dataset.

Featurization of patches using multiple conditional variational autoencoders. Once the pixels are pre-processed, VIMA converts each sample into a set of tissue patches of size 40 × 40 pixels. (Depending on cellular density, each tissue patch typically contains tens to hundreds of cells. As the tissue patches overlap, a 1 × 1-cm tissue fragment would yield 10,000 tissue patches with meta-marker information on 1 million pixels.) All patches for which fewer than 20% of the pixels contain tissue (as opposed to background) are then discarded.

VIMA then trains ten conditional variational autoencoders in parallel to each learn a C-dimensional latent representation from which it can reconstruct the tissue patches, where C = 100 by default. The loss function that is optimized is a standard variational autoencoder loss:

The loss function is optimized stochastically in the standard way using the reparameterization trick59. Because the runtime of the training process has non-trivial contributions both from backpropagation and from serving the training instances, training all ten autoencoders in parallel takes substantially less than ten times as long as training them in series. The autoencoders’ architecture (Supplementary Fig. 25) is a reduced ResNet35 adapted to 40 × 40 patches (rather than 224 × 224). The autoencoders are also conditional VAEs34: both the encoder and decoder are given access to sample-level covariates via a learned four-dimensional embedding wn for sample n that is a function of a one-hot encoding of sample ID together with any other covariates supplied. This is converted into four new spatially homogeneous channels by setting all spatial locations in the i-th new channel to wn i . These new channels are then concatenated to the model’s representation at each layer. The variational penalty then incentivizes the encoder to remove sample-specific information, with the decoder supplying it back during reconstruction. This method of incentivizing integration has been successfully used in single-cell integration60. In simulation, we show that performance does not strongly depend on β as long as it is not extremely small (Supplementary Fig. 20). Accordingly, in practice we simply set β = 10 −5 with the recommendation that if the patches are not well integrated across samples then β should be increased by one order of magnitude at a time until this is achieved. (We have not had to do this in the datasets analyzed in this paper.) We train the autoencoders using standard practice, with 80% of the patches used for training and 20% used for validation. We use a batch size of 256 patches, a default learning rate of 10−3 with an exponential decay parameter of 0.9 per epoch, Kullback–Leibler divergence warmup over the first 5 epochs, and 20 epochs of training with option to extend if the validation loss has not plateaued. These settings were uniform across all datasets processed.

Definition of microniches. Once the autoencoders are trained, they are each run on all P patches in the dataset whose tissue density (the fraction of pixels containing tissue) is greater than some threshold α to produce a C-dimensional vector zp for each patch p; α is set to 0.5 by default. Each set of embeddings zp is then used to construct a nearest-neighbor graph of all P patches using scanpy’s neighbors function61. The microniches are then defined similarly to how transcriptional neighborhoods are defined in our previous work in nonspatial single-cell analysis36. That is, we define one microniche for each patch p and each autoencoder e using the nearest-neighbor graph Ge generated by the patch fingerprints created by e: for every other patch p’, the degree of belonging to the microniche anchored at patch p is the probability that a random walk in Ge starting at patch p’ will arrive at patch

Applying the above procedure for each sample in the dataset allows us to build the MAT, which formally is an N × P × 10 tensor whose n,p,e-th entry equals the expected fraction of patches from sample n that would arrive at patch p after s steps in Ge (the relative abundance of microniche p in sample n according to the fingerprints generated by the autoencoder e). The MAT can be computed quickly using sparse matrix multiplication as the matrix Ae + I is sparse. As with previous work36, our software allows for covariates to be projected out of the MAT.

Statistical association testing. Given the MAT Q and a sample-level attribute of interest y, VIMA performs two types of association testing: a global association test, which is meant to assess for any aggregate relationship between abundance of the microniches as captured by Q and y, and a local association test, which is meant to find specific microniches whose abundance correlates with y. VIMA begins by standardizing Q along its second dimension (that is, each microniche is standardized). It then computes a matrix C of dimension 10 × P whose e,p-th entry is the correlation across samples between the phenotype y and the abundance of each sample in the p-th microniche according to autoencoder e. To compute the local test, VIMA then computes, for each patch p, a meta-analyzed correlation ρp using the ratio of the third to second moments:

which yields a single length-P vector ρ with one meta-analyzed correlation per patch. The motivation for this meta-analysis is that we would like to compute the average correlation across all ten autoencoders, but we want to allow for the possibility that for a given patch p, some autoencoders have learned more useful structure than others. We therefore weight our average by the square of each respective correlation. To assess statistical significance, VIMA then does the same procedure for a large number of random permutations of y. It then computes, for each potential value ρ∗ that might be used as a cutoff for statistical significance, an empirical estimate of the FDR at that threshold. That is, it naively estimates

To account for the presence of multiple samples from the same donor, which is common in spatial datasets, the permutation scheme used preserves the property that samples from the same donor have the same sample-level attribute. Null simulations To assess the calibration of VIMA, we performed simulations using a real spatial transcriptomics dataset from the Seattle Alzheimer’s

Disease Brain Cell Atlas (SEA-AD) dementia cohort48. This dataset consists of S = 75 postmortem medial temporal gyrus samples from N = 27 patients, 15 of whom had dementia. Each sample was profiled using MERFISH, yielding spatial information about M = 140 genes at single transcript resolution, with a total of 516 million transcripts profiled. For the simulation in Supplementary Fig. 3, we generated 500 simulates in which the samples were left unmodified and a random binary case−control label was assigned to each sample. We then quantified type I error at level α = 0.05 by computing the fraction of null simulates in which VIMA rejected the null hypothesis.

Non-null simulations To assess the power and spatial accuracy of VIMA, we downsampled the SEA-AD dementia cohort to just the samples that had at least 100 tissue patches that passed VIMA’s transcript-density-based quality control filter, choosing for each donor the sample with the most patches if multiple samples met this criterion for a single donor. This resulted in a set of S = 21 samples (with unique donors). We then created a case-associated tissue structure by arbitrarily choosing a 400 × 400-μm tissue patch from one of the samples and increasing the value of the second harmonized meta-marker in all pixels by 2 s.d. We then simulated two types of signals: (1) a ‘case-only’ signal, in which control samples were left unmodified and a tunable number of copies of this tissue structure, with Gaussian noise added to each pixel, were spiked into each case sample in random locations; and (2) an ‘enrichment’ signal, in which a fixed number of copies of this tissue structure, with Gaussian noise added to each pixel, were spiked into each case sample in random locations and a smaller but nonzero number were similarly spiked into each control sample at a specified, tunable ratio of abundance between cases and controls. For each signal, we generated 30 simulates at a number of different signal strengths determined either by the abundance of the structure in cases (in the ‘case-only’ scenario) or the ratio of abundance in cases to abundance in controls (in the ‘enrichment’ scenario). For each signal strength, we quantified power in the standard way at level 5%. We also quantified VIMA’s spatial accuracy as follows: for each simulate, we computed the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve obtained from using VIMA’s microniche coefficients to classify each patch as either containing the spiked-in signal or not. We then averaged this over all simulates at each signal strength. The results are shown in Supplementary Fig. 4.

Analyses of real data We analyzed three real datasets: synovial biopsies from patients with RA profiled with immunofluorescence microscopy (S = 27 samples from N = 22 donors, M = 7 markers profiled)38; colonic biopsies from patients with and without UC profiled with CODEX (S = 42 samples from N = 34 donors, M = 52 markers profiled)19; and postmortem medial temporal gyrus samples from patients with and without dementia profiled with MERFISH (S = 75 samples from N = 27 donors, M = 140 genes profiled)48. In addition to VIMA, we also analyzed these datasets with a suite of benchmarking methods: CellCharter22, STAGATE26, UTAG21, CAN- VAS32 and TissueMosaic33, a ‘patchwide average expression’ baseline in which each tissue patch was featurized by the patchwide average of the harmonized meta-markers generated by VIMA’s preprocessing, and a ‘patchwide cell-type abundance’ baseline in which each tissue patch was featurized by the relative abundances of each cell type in that tissue patch. These methods were chosen to represent a diversity of approaches to single-modality tissue annotation that are prevalent in the field, including both neural network-based and non-neural network-based methods, and including both methods that work from segmented cells as well as methods that work from raw expression data. Each method was run on each dataset with the following exceptions: in the RA dataset, we were unable to apply CellCharter, UTAG, TissueMosaic and the patchwide cell-type abundance baseline because we did not

Analysis of rheumatoid arthritis dataset. We obtained the RA dataset from the Accelerating Medicines Partnership Rheumatoid Arthritis and Systemic Lupus Erythematosus consortium. We pre-processed the data with the default preprocessing workflow described above, using the ratio between the summed intensity of all seven markers and the intensity of the auto-fluorescence channel to summarize the total amount of tissue signal in each pixel. After log-normalization, PCA across meta-pixels, and Harmony as described above, this resulted in five (harmonized) meta-markers per pixel, and a mask for each sample that defines which pixels are assumed to come from tissue. We then ran VIMA on the dataset with default settings, except that we set α (the fraction of pixels in a patch that must be non-empty for VIMA to include it in the case−control analysis) to 0.8 due to the difficulty accurately distinguishing tissue from nonspecific background staining in this dataset as well as the highly irregular borders of many of the samples. In addition to using VIMA, we also generated tissue annotations for this dataset using CANVAS32, STAGATE26 and our patchwide average expression baseline (the additional methods in our benchmarking suite all required cell segmentation, which was not available for this dataset; see above). For details of how these methods were applied, see ‘Details of benchmarking’ below. To compute the degree of sample integration in each method’s embedding for Fig. 2b, we constructed a nearest-neighbor graph on the spatial units used by each method using whatever embedding that method assigned to those spatial units and using scanpy’s default parameters. For each method, we then quantified, for each spatial unit, the perplexity of the distribution over samples induced by that unit’s neighbors in the graph, and divided this by the perplexity of the distribution over samples induced by all the spatial units in the graph; we refer to this as ‘relative perplexity across samples’. To apply PCA to VIMA’s MAT for Fig. 3a, we converted the MAT from a N × P × 10 tensor into an N × 10P matrix and applied standard PCA to the matrix. We note that in the future tensor decomposition could be used instead, which would give directions of variance explained by multiple autoencoders; however, we did not pursue this here. For the case−control analysis, we used each sample’s CTAP, determined using separate nonspatial single-cell RNA-seq. The six CTAPs are T, TB, TM, TF, EFM and F and reflect preponderances of various combinations of T cells (T), B cells (B), fibroblasts (F), endothelial cells (E) and myeloid cells (M). We defined a sample to be ‘stromal’ if it is in the union of all the fibroblast-containing CTAPs:

F ∗= F ∪TF ∪EFM.

and ‘immune’ otherwise. We applied VIMA’s case−control analysis to stromal status to obtain a global P value and a set of associated microniches at FDR 10%. To produce the benchmarking results in Fig. 3c, we ran an analogous case−control analysis using tissue annotations from the other three comparator methods used in this dataset. For each method, we clustered spatial units based on their embeddings, using the method’s native clustering when available or Leiden clustering with default parameters otherwise. For each cluster, we computed the squared correlation between its abundance across samples and the phenotype, derived P values via null permutations, and obtained a global P value using Bonferroni correction across clusters. We also evaluated alternative approaches: using the sum of squared correlations across the clusters as a global test statistic with permutation-based P values (Supplementary Fig. 22), harmonizing embeddings across

samples before testing (Supplementary Fig. 23), and applying VIMA’s microniche framework directly to each method’s embeddings (Supplementary Fig. 24). These yielded only modest improvements. To assess which markers have higher average intensity in VIMA’s stromal-associated patches, we computed the average intensity of each marker in each patch. We then estimated the distribution of each marker across all the patches identified by VIMA as typical of the stromal samples and across all the patches identified by VIMA as typical of the immune samples (Supplementary Fig. 5). We next clustered positively and negatively associated patches by restricting the VIMA nearest-neighbor graph to each set and applying Leiden clustering41 with resolution chosen to yield two clusters. We compared average marker levels as for stromal-associated patches (Supplementary Figs. 6 and 7). We then computed CTAP enrichment for each cluster by counting, for each CTAP with >50 represented patches, the number of associated patches in that cluster and calculating log ORs for cluster membership. Then, s.e. values were computed using the asymptotic variance formula for contingency tables (1/a + 1/b + 1/c + 1/d  where a, b, c, d  are the four counts used). For immune-associated patches, there were insufficient stromal CTAP patches to assess enrichment. For stromal-associated patches, enrichment was evaluated for all CTAPs, though only immune CTAPs showed appreciable enrichment (Supplementary Fig. 8).

Analysis of ulcerative colitis dataset. We obtained the UC dataset in tiff format from the authors of the original study19. In addition to spatial data, each patient also had metadata specifying whether they had UC or not, whether they were on a TNF inhibitor at the time of their biopsy, and whether they were on a TNF inhibitor in the past. In addition to the 52 CODEX markers, each sample also had 21 channels consisting of Hoechst stains that were used to register the markers across different rounds of imaging in the CODEX protocol. We noticed that these stains induced substantial inter-sample batch effects so we removed them before normalizing the pixel intensities in the dataset. We pre-processed the data with the default preprocessing workflow described above, using the summed intensity of all the CODEX markers and the nuclear stains to summarize the total amount of tissue signal in each pixel, but using only the CODEX markers for the dimensionality reduction from markers to meta-markers. This resulted in ten (harmonized) meta-markers per pixel, and a mask for each sample that defines which pixels are assumed to come from tissue. We then ran VIMA on the dataset with default settings to check for association to UC-versus-healthy status, removing from the case−control analysis (but not from the training of the autoencoder) any sample that either was on a TNF inhibitor or had been on one in the past to maximize the contrast between UC and healthy tissue. This resulted in a global P value for association as well as a set of microniches significantly associated (both positively and negatively) with UC status at FDR 10%. In addition to using VIMA, we also generated tissue annotations for this dataset using CANVAS32, STAGATE26, UTAG21, TissueMosaic33, our patchwide average expression baseline and our patchwide cell-type abundance baseline (CellCharter22, whose proteomics workflow uses trVAE62 to integrate the expression profiles of the cells, did not finish within our runtime limit of 3 days due to the trVAE step). For details of how these methods were applied, see ‘Details of benchmarking’ below. To assess which markers have higher average intensity in the UC-associated patches, we computed the average intensity of each marker in each patch. We then estimated the distribution of each marker across all the UC-associated patches identified by VIMA as well as the healthy-associated patches. To identify patches typical of treatment with TNF inhibition, we took only the patches found by VIMA to have a significant positive association with UC and re-built new nearest-neighbor graphs using the patch fingerprints of these patches. We then used these new nearest-neighbor graphs to define a new MAT and ran our association

We then repeated the same workflow described above to identify markers typical of the positively and negatively associated patches. We also clustered these patches into two clusters in the same way that we clustered associated patches in the RA dataset and recovered a similar association to TNFi status independent of the association to UC status (Supplementary Figs. 9 and 10). To show that the chronic/priorTNFi-versus-never/newTNFi signature was distinct from the UC-versus-healthy signature, we selected all the patches found to be significantly chronic/priorTNFi-associated and compared their UC microniche coefficients to those of the patches that were significantly never/newTNFi-associated (Supplementary Fig. 11). If the two signatures were similar, we might expect the chronic/priorTNFi-associated microniches to have lower correlations to UC on average than the never/newTNFi-associated patches; instead, we saw nearly identical distributions, with the median UC correlation actually being slightly higher among the chronic/priorTNFi-associated microniches.

Analysis of dementia dataset. We downloaded the dementia dataset from the SEA-AD website. In addition to spatial data, each patient was also labeled as either having dementia or not. To enable comparison to the local averaging paradigm as instantiated through local cell-type abundances, we performed cell segmentation on the data as described in ref. 63 and then annotated those cells using the Allen Institute’s Map- MyCells tool (https://portal.brain-map.org/atlases-and-data/bkp/mapmycells) using the matching ‘10x Human MTG SEA-AD (CCN20230505)’ reference taxonomy and the ‘SEA-AD Correlation Mapping’ algorithm. As a result, each cell was annotated as having a spatial location and a cell type at several specific cell-type resolutions. We pre-processed the data with the default preprocessing workflow described above, using the total transcript count per pixel to summarize the total amount of tissue signal in each pixel. This resulted in ten (harmonized) meta-markers per pixel, and a mask for each sample that defines which pixels are assumed to come from tissue. We then ran VIMA on the dataset with default settings to check for association to dementia versus non-dementia status, yielding a global P value for association and a set of significant microniches at FDR 5%. In addition to using VIMA, we also generated tissue annotations for this dataset using CANVAS32, STAGATE26, UTAG21, TissueMosaic33, CellCharter22, our patchwide average expression baseline and our patchwide cell-type abundance baseline. For details of how these methods were applied, see ‘Details of benchmarking’ below. To determine correspondence of associated microniches with cortical layers, we computed cell-type proportions per patch and defined layer 6b patches as those with ≥5% ‘L6b’ cells and layer 2/3 patches as those with ≥30% ‘L2/3 IT’ cells. To identify cell-type enrichment in dementia-associated patches relative to other layer 6b patches, we compared median proportions of the 24 annotated cell types and assessed significance by permuting association labels (dementia-associated versus not) of layer 6b patches within each donor to generate null distributions (Supplementary Table 4). To validate these findings, we defined layer 2/3 patches (>30% ‘L2/3 IT’) and oligodendrocyte-rich layer 6b patches (>5% ‘L6b’ and >10% oligodendrocytes), computed their proportions per sample, and compared cases and controls using a one-sided Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. We also clustered these patches as in the RA and UC analyses and examined spatial and compositional differences between clusters (Supplementary Figs. 13–15). For comparison to a nonspatial analysis, we represented each sample by its cell-type proportions and tested association with case–control status using correlation with permutation-based FDRs analogous to VIMA (Supplementary Fig. 12).

Benchmarking, ablations and simulations Details of benchmarking. We provide below details of how each method in our benchmarking suite was run, followed by details of how each method’s embedding was used for case–control analysis.

STAGATE. As STAGATE’s spatial unit is a visium-sized tissue region for which it is supplied with an average expression profile, we generated 100 × 100-μm patches for each dataset and computed the average expression profile of each patch. We then ran STAGATE with default parameters, rad_cutoff = 150 μm and n_epochs = 1,000.

CANVAS. We ran CANVAS’s preprocessing code directly on the 10-μm-resolution pixelated counts matrices generated by VIMA’s rasterization procedure, as the default 1-μm resolution either introduced prohibitive sparsity (MERFISH) or computational cost (CODEX and IF), while also reducing comparability to VIMA. We specified the average of all the channels as the ‘background’ channel per the documentation. We then trained the CANVAS model, stopping training at 200 epochs (~24 h of training) due to runtime constraints.

Patchwide average expression. For each VIMA patch, we computed the average of the harmonized meta-markers within that patch.

UTAG. We obtained segmented cells with cell-level expression data from the authors of the UC study and from the online portal associated with the dementia study, and we ran UTAG on these cells according to the ‘batch mode’ tutorial, setting max_dist = 15, and normalization_mode = ‘l1_norm’ per that tutorial.

CellCharter. We obtained segmented cells with cell-level expression data from the authors of the UC study and from the online portal associated with the Alzheimer’s disease study, and we ran CellCharter on these cells with default parameters and following the online tutorials associated with the method, which recommended integration of the cells with scVI64 for the spatial transcriptomic data and trVAE62 for the CODEX data; however, trVAE did not finish training on the UC dataset with default parameters in 3 days, and so we did not include CellCharter results for that dataset.

TissueMosaic. We obtained cell types from the authors of the UC study for the segmented cells in that study, and we used the MapMyCells tool as above to call cell types for the segmented cells in the Alzheimer’s disease study. We then gave these as input to TissueMosaic and trained the model with default parameters except for modest adjustments to the training schedule due to runtime considerations (num_workers = 16, param_momentum_epochs_end = 700, warm_up_epochs = 70, warm_down_epochs = 70, and max_epochs = 700) and global_size = 100 rather than 96 (after discussion with the authors, to match the Tissue- Mosaic patch size to VIMA’s patch size).

Patchwide cell-type abundances. We obtained cell types for segmented cells from the authors of the UC study, and we used the MapMyCells tool as above to call cell types for the segmented cells in the Alzheimer’s disease study. We then computed the relative abundance of each cell type in each of VIMA’s patches. To evaluate each method’s embedding, we clustered the spatial units generated by each method either using Leiden clustering with default parameters or, if available, using whatever clustering was performed by the method in question. We then produced an N × K matrix, where N is the number of samples and K is the number of clusters, whose n,k-th entry is the relative abundance of cluster k in sample n. We then computed the correlation Ck between the k-th cluster and the phenotype for each k. We produced one P value per cluster by comparing Ck to a null distribution obtained by permuting the sample labels while preserving identical labels for samples from the same donor. We then computed
